Sorting newest first, so old items sink out of sight.
troubleshooting: If counts look low, the open set exceeds the data row limit. Raise it to 2,000 in Settings or narrow the filter.
If the status filter shows a delegation warning, use separate not-equals conditions as shown rather than the in operator.
If the queue looks stale, reload on OnVisible and after each update.
If the gallery is slow, remove controls from the row template and keep the collection to the columns needed with ShowColumns.

build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.shortDescription: Split a long record across tabs such as Details, Activity and Files on one screen.
build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.fullDescription: Tabs keep a detailed record readable without several screens. One variable holds the selected tab, a horizontal gallery draws the tab bar, and each tab's content sits in a container that shows only when selected.
build-a-tabbed-request-detail-screen.problemStatement: A detail screen has become a long scroll of fields, comments and attachments, and users cannot find what they need.
whenToUse: Records with distinct groups of information
Screens that combine fields, history and files
Tablet and desktop layouts
whenNotToUse: Short records that fit on one view
Steps that must be completed in order, which suit a wizard
stepByStepInstructions: Create a context variable for the selected tab.
Add a horizontal gallery of tab labels that sets the variable.
Put each tab's controls in its own container and set Visible from the variable.
Load heavier data when its tab is first opened.
Keep shared buttons such as Save outside the tab containers.
commonMistakes: Separate screens per tab, which lose unsaved input when switching.
Loading every tab's data up front.
Validation errors on a hidden tab that the user cannot see.
troubleshooting: If inputs lose their values when switching tabs, they are being reset by a changing Default. Hiding a container does not clear its controls.
If a hidden tab's required field blocks saving, flag the tab with an error marker and switch to it.
If the tab bar overflows on phones, make the gallery scroll horizontally or use a dropdown below a width breakpoint.
If the tab is blank on open, pass locTab in Navigate or set the default in OnVisible.

build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.shortDescription: Design a request form that works on a phone: one column, large touch targets, the right keyboard and a fixed submit bar.
build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.fullDescription: Phone forms fail when they are shrunken desktop forms. This pattern uses a vertical auto-layout container, full-width inputs sized for touch, input types that bring up the right keyboard and a submit bar that stays in view.
build-a-compact-mobile-request-form.problemStatement: Field staff struggle with tiny controls, a keyboard that hides the input and a Submit button somewhere below the fold.
whenToUse: Apps used mainly on phones
Short capture forms completed on the move
Forms that include photos or location
whenNotToUse: Long data entry best done at a desk
Forms needing wide tables or side-by-side comparison
stepByStepInstructions: Lay the screen out as header, scrolling body and fixed footer.
Stack fields in one column with inputs at least 44 to 48 high and stretched to full width.
Set keyboard modes so number and email fields open the right keyboard.
Replace short dropdowns with tap buttons and pre-fill what you can.
Keep Submit in the footer, disabled until the minimum is entered, and clear the form after sending.
commonMistakes: Two columns of fields on a phone.
Small icons as the only way to act.
A submit button inside the scrolling area.
troubleshooting: If the keyboard covers the input, make sure the input sits inside a scrollable container so the player can move it into view.
If the numeric keyboard does not appear, set both Format and VirtualKeyboardMode on classic text inputs.
If the layout breaks in landscape, lock orientation in Settings or use auto-layout containers.
If photos are slow to upload, lower the camera resolution or use the Add picture control.

build-a-reusable-filter-panel.shortDescription: Add a slide-in filter panel with status, owner and date filters that apply together and can be cleared in one tap.
build-a-reusable-filter-panel.fullDescription: A filter panel keeps the main screen clean while offering several filters. This pattern holds the applied filters in one record variable, applies them in a single delegable Filter, and shows how many are active.
build-a-reusable-filter-panel.problemStatement: Filters are scattered across the top of the screen, each change reloads the gallery, and users cannot tell which filters are on.
whenToUse: Galleries with three or more filters
Phone layouts with little room
Filters that should apply together with an Apply button
whenNotToUse: One or two filters, which are fine inline
Data that cannot be filtered delegably and is too large to collect
stepByStepInstructions: Hold the applied filters in one record variable with defaults.
Build a panel container with the filter controls, Apply and Clear.
Copy control values into the record on Apply and close the panel.
Write the gallery's Filter so each condition is skipped when its filter is at the default.
Show a badge with the number of active filters.
commonMistakes: Binding the gallery directly to the panel's controls, so it reloads on every change.
Filter logic that is not delegable, such as the in operator on a column.
No indication that filters are active.
troubleshooting: If a delegation warning appears, test each condition on its own to find the one that is not delegable.
If the date filter misses the last day, compare with the day after the end date as shown.
If Clear does not reset a control, its Default must read from the filter record.
If filtering unassigned items misses rows, test the person column with AssignedTo.Email = Blank() or keep a text copy of the owner's email.

build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.shortDescription: Break a long form into steps on one screen, validate each step and review everything before submitting.
build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.fullDescription: A wizard keeps a long intake manageable. All steps live on one screen so input is never lost, a variable tracks the current step, each Next validates its step, and the last step shows a summary before one Patch.
build-a-multi-step-intake-wizard.problemStatement: A single long form is abandoned halfway, and a form split across screens loses data when users go back.
whenToUse: Intake forms with more than eight to ten fields
Forms where later questions depend on earlier answers
Processes that benefit from a review step
whenNotToUse: Short forms
Expert users who prefer everything on one page
stepByStepInstructions: Group the fields into three to five steps and define them in a table.
Place each step in its own container on one screen, shown by a step variable.
Add a progress indicator and a heading showing the step number.
Validate the current step before moving on.
Finish with a read-only review and a single Patch on submit.
commonMistakes: One screen per step, which loses input and repeats layout.
Validating only at the end, sending users back to hunt for errors.
No way to go back and change an earlier answer.
troubleshooting: If values vanish when moving between steps, a control's Default is tied to something that changes. Hidden containers keep their values.
If a skipped step still blocks submission, exclude its fields from the final checks.
If users lose work when the app closes, save a draft at each Next with Patch and a Draft status.
If the progress gallery shows numbers as decimals, wrap the number in Text().

build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.shortDescription: Let users add several line items to a collection, review and edit them, then save them all at once.
build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.fullDescription: Line items such as order lines or expense rows are easier to enter when nothing is saved until the user is ready. This pattern keeps the rows in a collection, supports add, edit and remove, shows a running total and writes everything with a bulk Patch.
build-a-collection-backed-review-screen.problemStatement: Each line is written to SharePoint as it is added, so abandoned entries leave orphan rows and every change waits on a network call.
whenToUse: Header and line item entry, such as orders, expenses and timesheets
Batches the user wants to check before committing
Up to a few hundred rows
whenNotToUse: Rows that other users must see immediately
Sessions long enough that losing unsaved rows would be costly, unless you add a draft save
stepByStepInstructions: Collect each new line into a collection with its own key.
Show the collection in a gallery with inline edit and remove.
Display a running count and total.
On save, create the header, then write all lines with one Patch.
Clear the collection only after a successful save.
commonMistakes: Writing each line to the list as it is added.
Clearing the collection before confirming the save worked.
Calling Patch once per row inside ForAll.
troubleshooting: If the bulk Patch fails with a type error, the record shape does not match the list's columns. Check names and types.
If only some lines are saved, compare the count in the list with the collection and offer a retry for the rest.
If inline edits do not stick, the row is being patched by a stale reference. Use ThisItem inside the gallery.
If users lose lines when the app closes, save the collection with SaveData on change and reload it with LoadData.

build-an-approval-history-timeline.shortDescription: Show a request's approval steps as a vertical timeline with who decided, when and what they said.
build-an-approval-history-timeline.fullDescription: A timeline answers where a request is and how it got there. This pattern reads decision rows from a history list, sorts them, and draws each as a dot, a connecting line and a card, with pending steps shown differently.
build-an-approval-history-timeline.problemStatement: Requesters cannot see which approval stage their request has reached or who it is waiting on.
whenToUse: Multi-stage approvals
Processes where requesters ask for status
History stored one row per decision
whenNotToUse: Single-step approvals, where one line of text is enough
Histories kept only as text in a notes column
build-an-approval-history-timeline.formulaOrCode:
List: Approval History
  Title | RequestId (Number, indexed) | Stage (Text) | StageOrder (Number) | Outcome (Choice: Pending, Approved, Rejected, Returned)
  ApproverName | ApproverEmail | DecidedOn (Date and time) | Comments

// Load for the open request
ClearCollect(
    colTimeline,
    SortByColumns(Filter('Approval History', RequestId = varRecord.ID), "StageOrder", SortOrder.Ascending)
)

// Vertical gallery: galTimeline.Items = colTimeline, flexible height, TemplatePadding 0

// Dot (circle)
Fill : Switch(ThisItem.Outcome.Value,
         "Approved", RGBA(16, 124, 16, 1),
         "Rejected", RGBA(196, 49, 75, 1),
         "Returned", RGBA(255, 185, 0, 1),
         RGBA(200, 198, 196, 1))                       // Pending

// Icon inside the dot
Icon : Switch(ThisItem.Outcome.Value, "Approved", Icon.Check, "Rejected", Icon.Cancel, "Returned", Icon.Reload, Icon.Clock)

// Connector line (thin rectangle below the dot)
Visible : ThisItem.StageOrder <> Last(colTimeline).StageOrder
Height  : Parent.TemplateHeight

// Card text
lblStage.Text  : ThisItem.Stage
lblWho.Text    : If(ThisItem.Outcome.Value = "Pending",
                    "Waiting for " & ThisItem.ApproverName,
                    ThisItem.Outcome.Value & " by " & ThisItem.ApproverName)
lblWhen.Text   : If(IsBlank(ThisItem.DecidedOn), "",
                    Text(ThisItem.DecidedOn, "d mmm yyyy, hh:mm") &
                    " (" & DateDiff(ThisItem.DecidedOn, Now(), TimeUnit.Days) & " days ago)")
lblComment.Text    : ThisItem.Comments
lblComment.Visible : !IsBlank(ThisItem.Comments)

// Summary above the timeline
lblSummary.Text :
    With({ pending: First(Filter(colTimeline, Outcome.Value = "Pending")) },
         If(IsBlank(pending), "All approval steps are complete.",
            "Currently with " & pending.ApproverName & " (" & pending.Stage & ")"))

// How long each stage took
DateDiff(LookUp(colTimeline, StageOrder = ThisItem.StageOrder - 1).DecidedOn, ThisItem.DecidedOn, TimeUnit.Hours) & " h"
stepByStepInstructions: Store each approval decision as a row in a history list, including pending steps.
Load the rows for the request, sorted by stage order.
Draw each row with a coloured dot, a connector line and a text card in a flexible-height gallery.
Show pending stages in grey with who they are waiting for.
Add a one-line summary of the current stage above the timeline.
commonMistakes: Showing only completed steps, so users cannot see what is still to come.
Fixed-height rows that cut off long comments.
Reading history from the list for every row instead of a collection.
troubleshooting: If the connector line has gaps, set the gallery's template padding to 0 and the line height to the template height.
If rows are in the wrong order, sort by a numeric stage order, not by title.
If comments are cut off, use a flexible-height gallery and auto-height labels.
If the filter shows a delegation warning, RequestId must be a number column compared with a number.

build-a-requester-self-service-screen.shortDescription: Give requesters one screen to track their requests and act on them: add information, withdraw or confirm completion.
build-a-requester-self-service-screen.fullDescription: Self-service reduces status emails. This pattern shows the requester's items with the next action expected of them, and offers only the actions that are valid for each status, each saved with a note.
build-a-requester-self-service-screen.problemStatement: Requesters email the team to ask for updates, add details or cancel, and the team re-keys those changes.
whenToUse: Request and ticket apps with a requester role
Processes where requesters must respond to queries
Teams that want fewer status emails
whenNotToUse: Processes where requesters must not change a submitted request
Apps used only by the fulfilment team
stepByStepInstructions: Load the user's own requests and flag the ones waiting on them.
Sort those to the top and say what is needed.
Offer add information, withdraw, confirm and reopen only in the statuses where each is valid.
Save each action as a status change with a note.
Describe the current status in plain language with the person it is waiting on.
commonMistakes: Letting requesters edit any field at any stage.
Showing internal status names that mean nothing to requesters.
Actions that change the status without telling the team.
troubleshooting: If requesters can act on other people's items, the filter is the only guard. Add list permissions or item-level permissions for real protection.
If the team is not told about new information, add a flow on the status change back to Submitted.
If the in operator against a list of statuses raises a warning, it is evaluated on the collection or a single record, which is fine.
If a requester cannot save, they need edit permission on their own items.

build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.shortDescription: Give administrators a safe place to find and fix bad records in bulk, with a preview and a log of what changed.
build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.fullDescription: Data problems recur: missing owners, invalid statuses, orphaned child rows. This pattern defines each known problem as a check with a query and a fix, shows the affected records first, applies the fix in bulk and logs it.
build-an-admin-data-repair-screen.problemStatement: Fixing bad data means editing rows one at a time in the list, with no record of what was changed.
whenToUse: Apps with recurring data quality problems
After a migration or schema change
Admins who are not comfortable with scripts
whenNotToUse: One-off fixes, which are quicker in grid view
Changes to thousands of rows, which suit a flow or script
stepByStepInstructions: List the known data problems and write a query for each.
Show the matching records for review before anything changes.
Enable the fix only after a preview of the same check.
Apply the fix as one bulk Patch using each record's ID.
Write the check name, count and record IDs to an admin log.
commonMistakes: Fixing without a preview.
No log, so nobody knows what was changed or when.
Running against more rows than the delegation limit returns and assuming everything is fixed.
troubleshooting: If the count stops at 500 or 2,000, more records remain. Run the check again until it returns none.
If the bulk Patch changes nothing, include the ID in each record so Patch knows which row to update.
If a filter on a blank person or date shows a warning, the list is being filtered locally. Narrow it with a delegable status filter first.
If a fix triggers many flow runs, add trigger conditions to those flows or pause them while repairing.

build-a-printable-request-summary.shortDescription: Create a clean, print-ready view of a record and save it as a PDF or send it to the printer.
build-a-printable-request-summary.fullDescription: Canvas apps can print a screen with Print(), or turn a screen or container into a PDF with the PDF function. This pattern builds a dedicated print layout, hides on-screen controls and offers both print and save to SharePoint.
build-a-printable-request-summary.problemStatement: Users take screenshots of the app to share or file a request, and the result includes buttons and cut-off text.
whenToUse: Records that must be filed, signed or shared outside the app
Summaries for meetings
Single-record output
whenNotToUse: Pixel-perfect or multi-record documents, which suit a Word template populated by a flow
Long tables that span many pages
stepByStepInstructions: Create a separate screen laid out like a page, with a white background and no navigation.
Bind labels and HTML text controls to the record, using auto height for long text.
Add a Print button that calls Print and hides itself using the screen's Printing property.
For a file, generate a PDF of the screen and pass it to a flow that saves it to a library.
Test with long content and with different page sizes.
commonMistakes: Printing the normal working screen with its buttons and scroll bars.
Using galleries for long tables, which cut off at the visible area.
Expecting Print to control paper size. The browser's print dialog does that.
troubleshooting: If content is cut off, use auto-height controls and set ExpandContainers to true in the PDF call.
If the PDF function is not recognised, enable it under Settings, in the upcoming features list for your app version.
If images are missing from the PDF, they are loaded from a source that needs sign-in. Use images stored in the app or in a column.
If Print does nothing on mobile, printing is supported in web browsers. Offer the PDF route on phones.

use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.shortDescription: Show progress while a flow runs from a button, block repeat taps, and handle the result or failure.
use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.fullDescription: Calling a flow from an app is synchronous: the formula waits for the response. This pattern sets a busy state around the call, captures the flow's response, handles errors and timeouts, and re-enables the screen.
use-a-loading-state-for-flow-calls.problemStatement: Users tap the button again because nothing seems to happen, the flow runs twice, and failures pass unnoticed.
whenToUse: Buttons that call a flow and wait for a result
Flows that take a few seconds
Actions that must not run twice
whenNotToUse: Long-running work over two minutes, which should be started and tracked through a status column instead
Fire-and-forget flows where the app does not need the result
stepByStepInstructions: Set a busy variable before calling the flow and clear it afterwards.
Store the flow's response in a variable.
Have the flow always respond, with a success flag and a message.
Wrap the call in IfError to catch connection failures and timeouts.
Disable the button while busy and once the record has moved on.
commonMistakes: A flow with no Respond action, so the app cannot tell what happened.
Leaving the busy state on when the call fails.
Waiting on a flow that takes minutes, which times out.
troubleshooting: If the call times out after about two minutes, the flow is too slow to wait for. Respond early and poll a status column.
If response fields are not recognised, remove and re-add the flow in the app after changing its Respond action.
If the flow ran but the app shows an error, a later action failed after the response was sent. Send the response last, or check the run history.
If the flow runs twice, the button was tapped twice before the busy state applied. Also guard in the flow with a status check.

use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.shortDescription: Navigate only after a save has succeeded, using the record Patch returns or the form's OnSuccess.
use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.fullDescription: Chaining Navigate straight after Patch moves the user on even when the save failed. This pattern captures the result, checks it, and then navigates with the saved record, including its new ID.
use-a-save-result-variable-for-navigatio.problemStatement: The app shows the confirmation screen although the record was never saved, or opens the detail screen with a blank record.
whenToUse: Any save followed by navigation
Screens that need the new item's ID
Custom forms and edit forms alike
whenNotToUse: Saves that keep the user on the same screen
Background saves where the result is not needed immediately
stepByStepInstructions: Store the result of Patch in a variable.
Wrap the save in IfError, or check Errors for the data source.
Navigate only in the success branch, passing the saved record.
With an edit form, navigate from OnSuccess, not from the button.
Use the saved record's values to choose where to go.
commonMistakes: Writing Patch(...); Navigate(...) so navigation happens regardless.
Calling SubmitForm and Navigate in the same button.
Reading the new ID from the gallery or by taking the last row of the list.
troubleshooting: If the next screen shows a blank record, the variable was set from the form's controls instead of the Patch result.
If navigation happens despite an error, the Navigate sits outside the IfError.
If OnSuccess never fires, validation failed. Show the form's Error in OnFailure.
If Last(DataSource) returns someone else's record, stop using it. The Patch result is the only reliable source of the new ID.

use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.shortDescription: Turn features on or off, for everyone or for a pilot group, from a SharePoint list without republishing.
use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.fullDescription: Feature flags let you ship a feature hidden, enable it for testers, then for everyone. This pattern stores flags in a list with an optional pilot audience, loads them once and exposes each as a boolean named formula.
use-app-settings-for-feature-flags.problemStatement: A half-finished feature blocks a release, or a new feature has to go to everyone at once with no way to switch it off.
whenToUse: Gradual rollouts and pilots
Features that may need to be turned off quickly
Different behaviour per environment
whenNotToUse: Security controls. A hidden button does not protect data.
Permanent configuration, where a settings list entry is clearer than a flag
stepByStepInstructions: Create a Feature Flags list with a name, an enabled switch and an optional pilot list.
Load it into a collection at start.
Expose each flag as a named formula that is true when enabled or when the user is in the pilot.
Use the formula in Visible, DisplayMode and If conditions.
Remove the flag and the old code path once a feature is fully released.
commonMistakes: Leaving flags in place for years until nobody knows what they do.
Defaulting a missing flag to on.
Using a flag to hide a feature that users must not access, without securing the data.
troubleshooting: If a flag change does not take effect, the app loads flags at start. Restart the app.
If a pilot user does not see the feature, check for spaces or a different email alias in the pilot list.
If the collection is empty on first use in a named formula, reference the list directly in the formula instead.
If testers and everyone else must differ per environment, keep a separate flags list in each environment's site.

use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.shortDescription: Hold files in a collection while the user fills in a new request, then upload them once the item exists.
use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.fullDescription: Attachments belong to an item, and a new item has no ID until it is saved. This pattern gathers files in a collection, shows them with remove buttons and size checks, and uploads them after the item is created, with the form control or a flow.
use-a-local-collection-for-draft-attachm.problemStatement: Users cannot attach files to a custom form for a new item, or the files vanish when the form is saved with Patch.
whenToUse: Custom forms that save with Patch
Photos captured in the app
Files that should go to a document library
whenNotToUse: Standard edit forms, where the attachments card and SubmitForm already work
Very large files that will not fit in device memory
stepByStepInstructions: Decide between reusing the form's attachment card with Patch, or your own collection with a flow.
Collect each chosen file or photo with a name and its content.
Show the files with a remove option and enforce count and size limits.
Create the item first and keep the returned record.
Upload each file against the new ID, then clear the collection.
commonMistakes: Expecting Patch to accept a table of files for the Attachments column without the form's Updates.
Uploading before the item exists.
Clearing the collection before the uploads finish.
troubleshooting: If the flow receives an empty file, pass the content from the attachment control's Value or the camera's Photo, inside a file record as shown.
If uploads are slow, each file is a separate flow run. Keep files small, or send all files to one flow run as an array.
If files over a certain size fail, check the list attachment limit of 250 MB and the practical memory limits of the device.
If the notification reports zero files, the collection was cleared first. Show the message before Clear, as in the sample.

use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.shortDescription: Show, hide and disable approve and reject buttons based on status and role, and say why an action is unavailable.
use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.fullDescription: Approval buttons should reflect what the current user can do right now. This pattern works out the allowed actions once from the item's status and the user's role, drives every button from that, and explains disabled states.
use-clear-button-states-for-approvals.problemStatement: Users see approve buttons on items they cannot approve, tap them and get an error, or see no buttons and do not know why.
whenToUse: Screens with approve, reject, return or withdraw actions
Several roles viewing the same record
Statuses that limit what can happen next
whenNotToUse: Screens with a single always-available action
As a replacement for server-side permission checks
stepByStepInstructions: List each action and the status and role that allow it.
Calculate a record of allowed actions when the screen opens and after each save.
Set each button's Visible and DisplayMode from that record.
Show a short sentence explaining why no action is available.
Re-check the item's current status when the button is pressed.
commonMistakes: Repeating slightly different conditions on each button.
Hiding everything with no explanation.
Trusting the button state alone, with no check at save time.
troubleshooting: If buttons do not update after a save, recalculate the allowed actions once the record variable changes.
If an approver sees disabled buttons, compare the approver email on the item with their sign-in.
If two people act at once, the re-check stops the second and refreshes their view.
If someone approves by editing the list directly, button states are not security. Lock down the list or move the write to a flow.

use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.shortDescription: Show a clear fallback such as Unassigned, and a default avatar, when a person column is empty.
use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.fullDescription: An empty person column is a blank record, so labels show nothing and photo lookups raise errors. This pattern uses Coalesce and IsBlank to show fallback text, initials or a generic icon, and handles multi-person columns.
use-fallback-text-for-blank-people-field.problemStatement: Galleries show empty gaps where an owner should be, and photo controls throw errors for rows with no person.
whenToUse: Galleries and detail screens showing assignees, approvers or managers
Optional person columns
User photos from Office 365 Users
whenNotToUse: Required person columns that are never empty
Screens where an empty value should stay visually empty
stepByStepInstructions: Wrap person display names in Coalesce with a fallback.
Style the fallback differently so missing owners stand out.
Guard photo lookups with a blank check and IfError.
Use IsEmpty for multi-person columns.
Hide contact actions when there is nobody to contact.
commonMistakes: Calling UserPhotoV2 with a blank email.
Testing a multi-person column with IsBlank instead of IsEmpty.
Showing the same fallback whether the item is new or long overdue for an owner.
troubleshooting: If the photo control shows an error icon, the user has no photo or the email is a guest's. IfError supplies the fallback.
If the gallery is slow, photo lookups are running for every row. Use initials in galleries and photos only on the detail screen.
If Coalesce still shows blank, the DisplayName is an empty string. Test the Email instead.
If the unassigned filter shows a delegation warning, add a text column that holds the owner's email and filter on that.

use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.shortDescription: Detect that someone else changed a record while the user had it open, and let them choose what to do.
use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.fullDescription: SharePoint rejects a Patch when the record has changed since it was loaded. This pattern checks the Modified time before saving, shows who changed the item and when, and offers reload or overwrite instead of a cryptic error.
use-a-conflict-warning-after-stale-edits.problemStatement: Two people edit the same item, and the second either overwrites the first without knowing or gets an error about a server conflict and loses their input.
whenToUse: Records edited by several people
Screens that stay open for a long time
Custom forms using Patch
whenNotToUse: Records only one person ever edits
Fields where the last write should always win
stepByStepInstructions: Store the record's Modified time when it is opened.
Before saving, read the item again and compare its Modified time.
If it is newer, show a dialog saying who changed it and when.
Offer reload, overwrite, or saving only the fields the user changed.
Update the stored time after every successful save.
commonMistakes: Patching the stale record from a variable, which triggers the conflict error.
Overwriting silently by always patching a fresh LookUp without comparing.
Showing the raw conflict error with no way forward.
troubleshooting: If every save reports a conflict, a flow updates the item right after each save. Refresh the stored Modified time after saving, or have the flow avoid touching the item.
If the conflict is never detected, the comparison uses a time captured after a refresh. Capture it only when the record is opened.
If the Editor name is blank, read it from the fresh LookUp rather than the gallery.
If the error text mentions an ETag mismatch, that is the same conflict reported by SharePoint. Use the fresh record as the Patch base.

use-a-reusable-validation-summary.shortDescription: Show every validation problem in one summary box at the top of the form, with a tap to jump to each field.
use-a-reusable-validation-summary.fullDescription: A validation summary tells users everything that needs fixing at once. This pattern defines the rules as a table, collects failures on save, lists them in a box and moves focus to the field when a message is tapped.
use-a-reusable-validation-summary.problemStatement: Users fix one error, press Save, and get the next one, several times in a row.
whenToUse: Forms with many fields or several sections
Accessibility requirements for clear error reporting
Custom forms and tabbed layouts
whenNotToUse: Two or three field forms, where inline messages are enough
Standard forms where the built-in card errors meet the need
stepByStepInstructions: Write every rule as a row with a key, a failing condition and a message.
On save, collect the failing rows.
Show them in a summary box above the form.
Move focus to the field when its message is tapped, switching tab if needed.
Drive inline borders and messages from the same collection.
commonMistakes: Showing errors before the user has tried to save.
Separate rule sets for the summary and the inline messages.
Messages that say a field is invalid without saying how to fix it.
troubleshooting: If SetFocus does nothing, the control is hidden or in a different container that is not visible. Switch tab first, as shown.
If the summary lingers after fixes, re-run validation on change.
If a date rule fires when the end date is empty, add a blank check to the condition.
If screen readers do not announce the summary, set the label's Live property.

use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.shortDescription: Define which status changes are allowed, and by whom, in one table that drives the buttons and the save check.
use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.fullDescription: A transition matrix lists each allowed move from one status to another with the role that may make it. The app reads it to offer only valid next steps and to validate before saving, so workflow rules live in one place.
use-a-status-transition-matrix-in-power-.problemStatement: Items jump from Draft to Closed, or move backwards, because any status can be picked from a dropdown.
whenToUse: Workflows with more than three statuses
Rules about who can move an item
Rules that change over time
whenNotToUse: Two-state items such as open and closed
Workflows enforced entirely in a flow or in Dataverse business process flows
stepByStepInstructions: List every allowed move with its starting status, target status and role.
Work out which roles the user holds for the open record.
Show a button for each transition that matches the current status and the user's roles.
On click, check the status has not changed, then Patch the new status with who and when.
Keep the matrix in a list if the business needs to change rules without a new app version.
commonMistakes: A free status dropdown alongside the matrix, which bypasses it.
Rules coded separately on each button.
Not checking the current status again at the moment of saving.
troubleshooting: If no buttons appear, the item's status text does not match any From value. Check spelling and spaces.
If a user sees too many actions, their roles are calculated too broadly.
If the status is changed in the list directly, the matrix is not enforced there. Restrict list editing or add a flow that reverts invalid moves.
If the gallery of actions flickers, calculate roles once per record instead of inside the gallery.

use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.shortDescription: Show users a read-only summary of what they entered and ask them to confirm before the record is submitted.
use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.fullDescription: A review step catches mistakes before they reach approvers. The same screen switches into review mode: inputs become read-only text, a summary highlights key values, and the user confirms or goes back to edit.
use-a-read-only-review-mode-before-submi.problemStatement: Requests are submitted with wrong amounts or dates, and correcting them after submission means a rejection and a resubmit.
whenToUse: Submissions that are hard to change afterwards
Forms with amounts, dates or declarations
Multi-step forms, as the final step
whenNotToUse: Quick forms where an edit after saving is easy
Forms that already save drafts and let users edit freely
stepByStepInstructions: Add a mode variable with Edit and Review values.
Validate when the user continues, then switch to review.
Show the entered values as read-only text, with consequences such as who will approve.
Require a confirmation tick before enabling Submit.
Let the user return to editing with their values intact, and save only on Submit.
commonMistakes: Saving the record before the review step, so cancelling leaves a submitted item.
A review screen that repeats the form without highlighting what matters.
Clearing the inputs when the user goes back to edit.
troubleshooting: If view-mode inputs are hard to read, use the separate summary container instead.
If values are lost on returning to edit, the review step is a different screen with its own controls. Keep both modes on one screen.
If Submit stays disabled, the confirmation checkbox was reset. Check its Reset is only called when going back.
If formatted values look wrong, such as dates in another language, pass a language tag to Text.

create-a-sharepoint-list-for-reusable-ap.shortDescription: Design one SharePoint list that holds dropdown values and lookups for several apps and flows.
create-a-sharepoint-list-for-reusable-ap.fullDescription: Reference data such as departments, categories and locations is better kept in a list than typed into choice columns or formulas. This pattern gives a schema that supports ordering, retiring values and extra attributes, and shows how apps and flows read it.
create-a-sharepoint-list-for-reusable-ap.problemStatement: The same list of departments is typed into three choice columns and two apps, and each copy is slightly different.
whenToUse: Dropdown values used by more than one app or list
Values that change or carry extra attributes such as an owner
Values the business should maintain without a maker
whenNotToUse: Three or four fixed values that never change, where a choice column is simpler
Large master data such as customers, which belongs in a proper system
create-a-sharepoint-list-for-reusable-ap.formulaOrCode:
List: Reference Data
  Title          Single line   the value users see                      (required)
  DataType       Choice        Department | Category | Location | Reason  (required, indexed)
  Code           Single line   stable key that never changes            (indexed, unique per type)
  SortOrder      Number        controls dropdown order, default 100
  IsActive       Yes/No        default Yes. Never delete, deactivate.
  ParentCode     Single line   for cascading values (Location -> Building)
  OwnerEmail     Single line   optional attribute, such as default assignee
  Notes          Multiple lines

Views
  By type       : group by DataType, sort by SortOrder
  Inactive      : IsActive equals No

Permissions
  Everyone: Read       Data stewards: Edit       (break inheritance on this list only)

Power Apps
  // load once
  ClearCollect(colRef, Filter('Reference Data', IsActive = true));
  // dropdown
  ddDepartment.Items : SortByColumns(Filter(colRef, DataType.Value = "Department"), "SortOrder", SortOrder.Ascending, "Title", SortOrder.Ascending)
  // cascading
  ddBuilding.Items   : Filter(colRef, DataType.Value = "Building" && ParentCode = ddLocation.Selected.Code)
  // save the stable code and the label
  Patch(Requests, Defaults(Requests), { DepartmentCode: ddDepartment.Selected.Code, DepartmentName: ddDepartment.Selected.Title })

Power Automate
  Get items   Filter Query: DataType eq 'Department' and IsActive eq 1    Order By: SortOrder

One list or several?
  One list with a type column suits small sets with the same shape.
  Give a set its own list when it needs its own columns or permissions, or passes a few hundred rows.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the list with a type column, a stable code, sort order and an active flag.
Index the type and code columns.
Give most users read access and a small group edit access.
Load active rows into a collection in each app and filter by type.
Save the code as well as the label on transactional records.
commonMistakes: Deleting a value that old records still use. Deactivate it instead.
Saving only the label, so renaming a value breaks reports.
No sort order, so dropdowns appear in creation order.
troubleshooting: If a dropdown is missing values, the list has more rows than the app's data row limit. Filter by type in the query rather than after loading.
If a renamed value does not show in an app, the app caches reference data at start. Restart it.
If users cannot see dropdown values, they lack read permission on the reference list.
If a lookup column is preferred to text codes, remember lookups count towards the 12-column lookup limit in views.

design-a-sharepoint-audit-history-list.shortDescription: Design a list that records who changed what and when on another list, sized and indexed so it stays usable as it grows.
design-a-sharepoint-audit-history-list.fullDescription: An audit history list receives one row per change from a flow or app. Because it grows quickly, the design matters: narrow columns, the right indexes, restricted permissions and a plan for archiving.
design-a-sharepoint-audit-history-list.problemStatement: Version history shows changes one item at a time and cannot answer questions such as who changed any status last month.
whenToUse: Changes that must be reported across items
Processes measured on time spent in each status
Evidence for audits
whenNotToUse: Needs met by version history on the item
Regulated audit trails, which should use Microsoft Purview audit logs
design-a-sharepoint-audit-history-list.formulaOrCode:
List: Change History
  Title          Single line    short description, e.g. "Status: New -> In progress"
  SourceList     Single line    name of the list that changed            (indexed)
  SourceItemId   Number         ID of the changed item                   (indexed)
  FieldName      Single line    column that changed                      (indexed)
  OldValue       Multiple lines (plain)
  NewValue       Multiple lines (plain)
  ChangedByEmail Single line    text, not a person column                (indexed)
  ChangedOn      Date and time                                           (indexed)
  ChangeSource   Choice         App | Flow | List edit | Import
  CorrelationId  Single line    groups several field changes from one save

Why text instead of person and lookup columns
  Person and lookup columns count towards the 12-lookup view limit, slow large lists
  and break when a user account is deleted. Text keeps the record intact.

List settings
  Versioning: off (rows are never edited)        Attachments: off
  Item-level permissions: Read all items / Create and edit: None (set in Advanced settings)
  Permissions: flow owner account Contribute, auditors Read, everyone else no access

Indexes: create them while the list is small. Above 5,000 items new indexes can fail.

Views (each filtered on an indexed column first)
  Last 30 days : ChangedOn >= [Today]-30, sort ChangedOn descending
  By item      : open with ?FilterField1=SourceItemId&FilterValue1=123
  Status only  : FieldName = Status

Writing rows from a flow (When an item is created or modified)
  Create item: Title, SourceList, SourceItemId = triggerBody()?['ID'], FieldName = 'Status',
               OldValue, NewValue, ChangedByEmail = triggerBody()?['Editor']?['Email'], ChangedOn = triggerBody()?['Modified']

Retention
  Yearly: move rows older than 24 months to an archive list or export to CSV in a library, then delete.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the list with text and number columns for the source, field, values, person and time.
Add indexes to the source item ID, field name, changed on and changed by columns straight away.
Turn off versioning and attachments, and restrict who can read it.
Write rows from a flow on the source list or from the app at save time.
Plan how old rows will be archived.
commonMistakes: Using person and lookup columns, which slow the list and hit view limits.
Adding indexes after the list has passed 5,000 items.
Letting ordinary users edit or delete history rows.
troubleshooting: If views fail with a threshold message, the first filter in the view is not on an indexed column.
If the flow's own update creates extra history rows, add a trigger condition so it runs only on real changes.
If ChangedBy shows the flow owner, read the Editor from the trigger instead of the connection.
If the list is nearing the practical limit for comfortable use, archive by year.

create-a-sharepoint-environment-inventor.shortDescription: Keep a register of the SharePoint sites, lists, apps and flows that make up a solution, with owners and review dates.
create-a-sharepoint-environment-inventor.fullDescription: Solutions built on SharePoint spread across sites, lists, apps and flows that nobody has listed. An inventory list records each asset with its owner, purpose and dependencies, so support and change planning do not rely on memory.
create-a-sharepoint-environment-inventor.problemStatement: When a maker leaves, nobody knows which lists and flows their apps depend on, or which can be retired.
whenToUse: Departments running several SharePoint-based solutions
Before a migration or tenant clean-up
Handing solutions over to a support team
whenNotToUse: A single small solution with one owner
Tenants already using the Center of Excellence toolkit inventory for apps and flows
create-a-sharepoint-environment-inventor.formulaOrCode:
List: Solution Inventory
  Title            Single line   asset name
  AssetType        Choice        Site | List | Library | Canvas app | Flow | Page | Power BI report
  Solution         Single line   the business solution it belongs to       (indexed)
  Url              Hyperlink     direct link to the asset
  Environment      Choice        Production | Test | Development
  BusinessOwner    Person        accountable for the process
  TechnicalOwner   Person        maintains it
  BackupOwner      Person
  Purpose          Multiple lines
  DependsOn        Multiple lines   other assets this one needs (list names, connections)
  Connections      Single line   e.g. SharePoint, Outlook, Approvals
  ServiceAccount   Single line   account that owns flows or connections
  DataSensitivity  Choice        Public | Internal | Confidential
  Status           Choice        Active | Being replaced | Retired
  LastReviewed     Date
  NextReview       Date          (indexed)

Views
  By solution     : group by Solution, then AssetType
  No backup owner : BackupOwner is empty
  Review due      : NextReview <= [Today]+30
  Retired         : Status = Retired

Filling it in
  Sites and lists : Site contents, or PnP PowerShell: Get-PnPList | Select Title, ItemCount, LastItemUserModifiedDate
  Apps and flows  : Power Platform admin center exports, or the Power Apps / Power Automate "for Admins" connectors
  Add each asset's owner by asking, not by assuming the creator still owns it.

Review reminder flow (monthly)
  Get items: NextReview le '@{addDays(utcNow(), 30, 'yyyy-MM-dd')}' and Status eq 'Active'
  Email TechnicalOwner with a link to the row; on completion set LastReviewed and move NextReview on 6 months.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the inventory list with asset type, solution, owners, dependencies and review dates.
List every site, list, app and flow in each solution, starting from exports where possible.
Confirm a business owner, a technical owner and a backup for each.
Record dependencies and the account that owns connections.
Review each entry twice a year with a reminder flow.
commonMistakes: Listing assets without owners.
Recording apps but not the lists and flows they depend on.
Building the inventory once and never reviewing it.
troubleshooting: If the inventory is always out of date, tie updates to your change process so no release happens without an inventory entry.
If owners have left, the person column shows a deleted user. Review the No backup owner view regularly.
If the list becomes long, split by solution with a view each rather than separate lists.
If you need automatic discovery, look at the Center of Excellence starter kit, which inventories apps and flows across environments.

document-sharepoint-list-ownership-and-s.shortDescription: Record who owns each business-critical list, who supports it and what to do when it breaks, where users can find it.
document-sharepoint-list-ownership-and-s.fullDescription: A list that runs a process needs a named owner and a support route. This pattern puts a short ownership record on the list itself and in a central register, covering contacts, what may be changed and how to raise a problem.
document-sharepoint-list-ownership-and-s.problemStatement: When a list or its app misbehaves, users do not know who to tell, and well-meaning site owners change columns that an app depends on.
whenToUse: Lists behind Power Apps or flows
Lists edited by many people
Sites with several owners
whenNotToUse: Personal or short-lived lists
Lists fully documented in an existing service catalogue
document-sharepoint-list-ownership-and-s.formulaOrCode:
1. On the list itself: Settings > List name, description and navigation
   Description (shows under the list title):
   "Owned by Facilities Operations. Used by the Facilities Request app. Do not change columns without
    contacting facilities-apps@contoso.com."

2. Ownership record (one item per list in a "List Register", or a page in the site)
   List name          : Facilities Requests
   URL                : https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/facilities/Lists/Requests
   Business owner     : decides what the process should do
   Technical owner    : maintains the list, app and flows
   Backup owner       : covers absence
   Support contact    : shared mailbox or Teams channel, not a person
   Support hours      : Mon-Fri 08:00-17:00
   Used by            : Facilities Request app, "Request approval" flow, monthly Power BI report
   Safe to change     : views, choice values in Category
   Ask first          : adding, renaming or deleting columns; permissions; list name or URL
   Data retention     : closed requests kept 3 years
   Backup and restore : recycle bin 93 days; version history 50 versions
   Last reviewed      : date

3. Tell users how to report a problem
   A "Report a problem" link in the app and on the list's site page:
   mailto:facilities-apps@contoso.com?subject=Facilities%20Requests%20problem

4. Column descriptions for columns the app depends on
   "Used by the Facilities Request app. Do not rename."

5. What breaks if columns change
   Rename a column  : display name changes are safe; the internal name stays the same
   Delete a column  : apps and flows that reference it fail
   Change a type    : not possible for most types; recreating it breaks references
   Required = Yes   : Patch and flows that do not set it start failing
stepByStepInstructions: Add a description to the list that names the owning team and support contact.
Create an ownership record with business, technical and backup owners.
List what depends on the list and which changes need agreement.
Add descriptions to columns that apps and flows rely on.
Give users a clear way to report problems and review the record yearly.
commonMistakes: Naming one person with no backup.
Keeping the documentation somewhere users never look.
Not saying which changes are safe, so every change is either blocked or risky.
troubleshooting: If people still change columns, limit who has Edit or Design permission on the list. Contribute cannot change columns.
If support requests go to an individual who has left, switch the contact to a shared mailbox.
If nobody will accept ownership, that is a signal to retire the list or escalate.
If the description does not show, it appears in the classic header and list information pane. Add the same text to the site page.

use-managed-metadata-vs-choice-fields.shortDescription: Decide between a choice column, a lookup and managed metadata, with the trade-offs that matter for Power Apps and Power Automate.
use-managed-metadata-vs-choice-fields.fullDescription: Choice columns are simple and work everywhere. Managed metadata gives one central, hierarchical set of terms across sites but is awkward in Power Apps and flows. This pattern sets out when each fits and what to expect.
use-managed-metadata-vs-choice-fields.problemStatement: A team picks managed metadata for consistency, then finds its Power App cannot filter on it delegably and Patch needs a complex record.
whenToUse: Choosing a column type for categories, departments or document types
Lists that Power Apps or flows will read and write
Tagging that must be consistent across many sites
whenNotToUse: Free-text values
Data with many attributes per value, which needs a lookup list
use-managed-metadata-vs-choice-fields.formulaOrCode:
Comparison
                        Choice              Lookup                 Managed metadata
  Where values live     in the column       another list           central term store
  Shared across sites   no (unless a site   same site only         yes, tenant-wide
                        column via hub)
  Hierarchy             no                  via extra column       yes
  Synonyms, languages   no                  no                     yes
  Who maintains         list owner          list contributors      term store managers
  Power Apps filter     delegable (=)       delegable on Id        not delegable
  Power Apps Patch      { Value: "x" }      { Id: 1, Value: "x" }  record with TermGuid, Label, WssId, Path, Value
  Flow filter query     Col eq 'x'          ColId eq 1             limited; TaxCatchAll workarounds
  Counts to lookup      no                  yes (12 per view)      yes (12 per view)
    threshold
  Search refiners       basic               basic                  strong

Rules of thumb
  Fewer than about 20 values, one list, used in apps or flows     -> Choice
  Values with attributes (owner, code, active flag), one site     -> Lookup list, or text codes from a reference list
  Enterprise taxonomy, document libraries, search and navigation  -> Managed metadata

Patching managed metadata from Power Apps (when you must)
  Patch(Documents, varRecord, {
      DocType: {
          '@odata.type': "#Microsoft.Azure.Connectors.SharePoint.SPListExpandedTaxonomy",
          Label: ddDocType.Selected.Label,
          TermGuid: ddDocType.Selected.TermGuid,
          WssId: 0,
          Path: "",
          Value: ddDocType.Selected.Label & "|" & ddDocType.Selected.TermGuid
      }
  })
  // Items for the dropdown: Choices(Documents.DocType)

Middle ground
  Keep managed metadata on the library for search and compliance, and add a plain text column
  that a flow fills with the term label. Apps and flows filter on the text column.
stepByStepInstructions: List where the column will be used: views, search, apps and flows.
Count the values and decide whether they need hierarchy or sharing across sites.
Choose a choice column for small local sets used in apps.
Choose managed metadata for tenant-wide taxonomy, mainly on document libraries.
Where an app must filter on managed metadata, mirror the label into a text column.
commonMistakes: Choosing managed metadata for a simple app dropdown.
Ignoring the lookup threshold when adding several metadata columns to one view.
Expecting to convert a choice column to managed metadata later without recreating it.
troubleshooting: If a Power Apps filter on a metadata column shows a delegation warning, it cannot be fixed on that column. Filter on a mirrored text column.
If Patch fails on a metadata column, check the TermGuid and the Value format of label, vertical bar, GUID.
If a flow's Get items cannot filter on the term, filter on the mirrored text column or use the TaxCatchAll approach in a REST call.
If views fail on a large library, there are more than 12 lookup-type columns in the view, counting metadata and person columns.

create-a-sharepoint-project-workspace-te.shortDescription: Build a standard project site once, with lists, libraries and pages, and reuse it for every new project.
create-a-sharepoint-project-workspace-te.fullDescription: A project workspace template gives every project the same structure: a document library with standard folders or metadata, risk and issue lists, a home page and navigation. Site templates, formerly site designs, apply that structure to new sites.
create-a-sharepoint-project-workspace-te.problemStatement: Every project site is built differently, so people cannot find things and portfolio reporting has no common lists to read.
whenToUse: PMOs and teams that start projects regularly
Reporting that needs the same lists on each project
Sites created by a provisioning request
whenNotToUse: One-off sites
Projects that live entirely in Microsoft Teams channels with no extra structure
create-a-sharepoint-project-workspace-te.formulaOrCode:
Standard contents
  Site type     : Team site connected to a Microsoft 365 group (one group per project)
  Library       : Project Documents  with columns Phase (Choice), DocumentType (Choice), plus views by phase
  Lists         : Risks, Issues, Decisions, Actions, Milestones (same columns on every site)
  Home page     : project summary, milestones web part, recent documents, key contacts
  Navigation    : Home | Documents | Plan | Risks & Issues | Decisions | Team
  Hub           : associate with the "Projects" hub for shared navigation and roll-up

Option 1: site template (site script), repeatable and central
  1. Build one model site by hand.
  2. Extract a script from it (PnP PowerShell or SharePoint Online Management Shell):
       Get-SPOSiteScriptFromWeb -WebUrl https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/project-model
           -IncludeLists ("Lists/Risks", "Lists/Issues", "Lists/Decisions") -IncludeBranding -IncludeTheme
  3. Register it:
       Add-SPOSiteScript -Title "Project workspace" -Content $script
       Add-SPOSiteDesign -Title "Project workspace" -WebTemplate "64" -SiteScripts <script id>
  4. New sites: Settings > Apply a site template > From your organization

  Site script actions used: createSPList (with addSPField, addSPView), addNavLink, applyTheme,
  joinHubSite, triggerFlow (calls a flow for steps the script cannot do)

Option 2: list templates only
  Create each list "From existing list" pointing at the model site. Quick, with no scripting.

Option 3: PnP provisioning template, for pages and web parts as well
  Get-PnPSiteTemplate -Out project.xml     Invoke-PnPSiteTemplate -Path project.xml

Portfolio roll-up
  Because every site has the same Risks list, a flow or Power BI can read them all through the hub.

Naming
  Site URL: /sites/prj-<code>      Group name: PRJ <code> <short name>
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the standard lists, columns, library structure and navigation.
Build one model site and test it with a real project.
Capture it as a site template, or use list templates for a lighter approach.
Apply the template when each new project site is created.
Associate project sites with a hub so navigation and reporting are shared.
commonMistakes: Copying an old project site, which carries its data and permissions.
A template so heavy that small projects ignore it.
Changing the model site and expecting existing project sites to update.
troubleshooting: If the template does not appear under From your organization, check its scope and that it was registered for the right site type, 64 for team sites.
If pages and web parts are missing, site scripts do not carry them. Use a PnP provisioning template or a flow step.
If existing sites need a new column, apply an updated script to them or add it with a flow. Templates do not update sites after creation.
If list columns differ between sites, portfolio reports break. Lock list design to site owners in the PMO.

build-a-sharepoint-issue-list-view-set.shortDescription: Create the standard set of views an issue list needs: mine, open by priority, overdue, unassigned and recently closed.
build-a-sharepoint-issue-list-view-set.fullDescription: One All Items view does not serve a team. This pattern defines an issue list's columns and a set of filtered, sorted views for the questions people ask every day, each built so it stays fast as the list grows.
build-a-sharepoint-issue-list-view-set.problemStatement: Everyone works from All Items, scrolling and filtering by hand, and overdue or unassigned issues go unnoticed.
whenToUse: Issue, risk, action and defect lists
Lists used directly in SharePoint or Teams
Teams of more than two or three people
whenNotToUse: Lists only ever used through a Power App
Lists with a handful of items
build-a-sharepoint-issue-list-view-set.formulaOrCode:
Columns
  Title | Status (Choice: New, In progress, Blocked, Resolved, Closed)        (indexed)
  Priority (Choice: Low, Medium, High, Critical)                               (indexed)
  AssignedTo (Person)                                                          (indexed)
  DueDate (Date)                                                               (indexed)
  Category (Choice) | ResolvedOn (Date) | Resolution (Multiple lines)

Views
  1. My open issues     (default)
     Filter : AssignedTo = [Me]  AND  Status <> Closed  AND  Status <> Resolved
     Sort   : DueDate ascending

  2. Open by priority
     Filter : Status <> Closed AND Status <> Resolved
     Group  : Priority        Sort: DueDate ascending
     Tip    : name choices "1 - Critical", "2 - High" so groups sort in the right order

  3. Overdue
     Filter : DueDate < [Today]  AND  Status <> Closed  AND  Status <> Resolved
     Sort   : DueDate ascending

  4. Unassigned
     Filter : AssignedTo is empty  AND  Status = New
     Sort   : Created ascending

  5. Blocked
     Filter : Status = Blocked           Sort: Modified ascending

  6. Recently closed
     Filter : Status = Closed  AND  ResolvedOn >= [Today]-14
     Sort   : ResolvedOn descending

  7. Board (optional)   Board view grouped by Status for drag and drop

Keep every view fast
  Put the most selective indexed column first in the filter.
  Use AND between conditions. An OR on the first condition stops the index being used.
  Limit columns to what the view needs, and keep person and lookup columns under 12.

Formatting
  Format the DueDate column to turn red when overdue, and Status as a coloured pill.

Share a view: copy its URL, or pin it as a tab in the team's Teams channel.
stepByStepInstructions: Add status, priority, assignee and due date columns and index them.
Create a personal default view filtered on [Me] and open statuses.
Add views for overdue, unassigned, blocked and recently closed items.
Group the open view by priority with choice names that sort correctly.
Apply column formatting for due dates and status, and pin key views in Teams.
commonMistakes: Leaving All Items as the default view.
Filtering with OR as the first condition on a large list.
Views with every column shown.
troubleshooting: If a view shows a threshold error, its first filter is not on an indexed column or uses OR.
If [Today] filters do not update, they do in views. In calculated columns they do not, so keep date logic in the view filter.
If My open issues is empty for someone, items are assigned to a group rather than to them. [Me] matches individuals.
If priority groups sort alphabetically, prefix the choice values with numbers.

create-a-default-view-for-active-work-on.shortDescription: Make the list open on active items only, so closed and archived rows stay out of the way and the view stays fast.
create-a-default-view-for-active-work-on.fullDescription: A list's default view sets how people experience it. Filtering it to active work, on an indexed column, keeps the list quick and relevant however large the history becomes, while other views keep the history reachable.
create-a-default-view-for-active-work-on.problemStatement: The list opens on thousands of rows going back years, takes a long time to load and buries current work.
whenToUse: Lists that keep closed or completed items
Lists approaching or beyond 5,000 items
Lists opened directly by users
whenNotToUse: Reference lists where every row is current
Lists small enough that filtering adds nothing
create-a-default-view-for-active-work-on.formulaOrCode:
1. Choose what "active" means and make it filterable
   Option A: Status column          Active = Status is not Closed, Cancelled or Archived
   Option B: IsActive (Yes/No)      set to No by a flow when the item closes. Simplest to filter.
   Option C: date window            Modified >= [Today]-90

2. Index the column you will filter on
   List settings > Indexed columns > Create a new index   (do this before the list passes 5,000 items)

3. Create the view
   Name    : Active
   Filter  : IsActive is equal to Yes
             (or: Status is not equal to Closed AND Status is not equal to Cancelled)
   Sort    : Modified descending
   Columns : 6 to 8 that people need at a glance
   Tick "Make this the default view"

4. Keep history reachable
   View "Closed this year" : IsActive = No AND ClosedOn >= start of year (enter the date, or use [Today]-365)
   View "All items"        : keep it, but not as the default. On large lists give it an indexed filter too.

5. Set the flag automatically (flow: when an item is modified)
   Trigger condition:
     @and(equals(triggerBody()?['Status']?['Value'], 'Closed'), equals(triggerBody()?['IsActive'], true))
   Update item: IsActive = No, ClosedOn = utcNow()

6. Point other things at the active view
   Site navigation link and Teams tab : the Active view URL
   Power Apps                         : Filter(Requests, IsActive = true)     // delegable
   Power Automate                     : Filter Query: IsActive eq 1

Why "not equal to" can be slower
  On very large lists, equals on an indexed Yes/No or choice column is the most reliable filter.
  That is the case for an IsActive flag over two not-equal conditions.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide how active items are identified: a status, a flag or a date window.
Index that column while the list is still small.
Create a view filtered to active items, sorted by most recently modified, and make it the default.
Add views that reach closed and historical items.
Set the active flag with a flow when items close, and point navigation and apps at the active filter.
commonMistakes: Filtering the default view on a column with no index.
Deleting the route to historical items altogether.
Relying on users to tick an archive box by hand.
troubleshooting: If the view still fails on a large list, the filter must reduce results below 5,000 using an indexed column in its first condition.
If closed items still appear, the flow did not set the flag. Check its trigger condition and run history.
If creating the index fails, the list is already over the threshold. Do it out of hours or reduce the list first.
If users land on All Items from an old bookmark, replace navigation links with the new view's URL.

govern-sharepoint-list-version-history.shortDescription: Set sensible version limits on lists and libraries, and know how to review and restore versions.
govern-sharepoint-list-version-history.fullDescription: Version history protects against mistakes, and uses storage. This pattern covers which settings to choose for lists and libraries, how versions behave with flows and apps, and how to restore or trim them.
govern-sharepoint-list-version-history.problemStatement: Versioning is off on a list that matters, so a bad edit cannot be undone, or it is unlimited on a busy library and storage is running out.
whenToUse: Lists that hold business records
Libraries with frequently edited documents
Sites near their storage quota
whenNotToUse: Log and history lists where rows are never edited
Temporary lists
govern-sharepoint-list-version-history.formulaOrCode:
Settings: List settings > Versioning settings

Recommended starting points
  Business list (requests, registers)   : versions On, keep 50
  Audit / log list (append only)        : versions Off
  Document library, normal use          : major versions, keep 100 (or automatic limits)
  Document library with approval        : major and minor, keep 50 major, drafts for 5 major
  Large media library                   : keep 5 to 10

Tenant and site defaults (libraries)
  SharePoint admin center > Settings > Version history limits
    Automatic : SharePoint trims older versions on a schedule based on age and activity
    Manual    : set a count and optional expiry
  PowerShell : Set-SPOTenant -EnableAutoExpirationVersionTrim $true
               Set-SPOSite -Identity <url> -EnableAutoExpirationVersionTrim $true

What creates a version
  Each save of an item or its properties. A flow that updates an item after every user edit
  doubles the version count. Combine the flow's changes into one Update item where possible.
  Power Apps Patch calls: one version per Patch. Two Patches on save = two versions.

Review and restore
  Item > ... > Version history > pick a version > Restore
  Restoring creates a new version. Nothing is lost.
  Deleted items: Recycle bin for 93 days, then the second-stage bin within the same period.

See what changed (list view)
  Version history shows only the fields that changed in each version.
  Multi-line columns with "Append changes" need versioning On to work at all.

Trim existing versions
  New limits apply as items are next edited. To trim now:
    New-SPOSiteFileVersionBatchDeleteJob -Identity <site url> -MajorVersionLimit 50 -MajorWithMinorVersionsLimit 0
  Check storage first: Site settings > Storage metrics.

Compliance
  If retention labels or holds apply, versions are kept regardless of these limits.
stepByStepInstructions: Check current versioning settings on each important list and library.
Turn versioning on for business lists with a limit of about 50.
Turn it off for append-only log lists.
Set library limits to match how documents are edited, or use automatic limits.
Show owners how to view and restore versions, and review storage each quarter.
commonMistakes: Unlimited versions on a library of large files.
Versioning off on a list that people edit all day.
Flows that update items repeatedly and multiply versions.
troubleshooting: If storage did not drop after lowering the limit, limits apply on the next edit. Run a trim job.
If Append changes text has disappeared, versioning was turned off. Turn it back on. Earlier entries may be lost.
If a restore does not bring back a deleted column's data, column deletion is not versioned. Restore the column from the recycle bin within 93 days.
If versions grow quickly, look for a flow or app writing the item more than once per save.

create-a-document-review-library-pattern.shortDescription: Set up a library where documents move from draft through review to approved, with status, reviewers and due dates as columns.
create-a-document-review-library-pattern.fullDescription: A review library adds a few columns and views to a standard library so everyone can see what is in draft, what is waiting for whom, and what is approved. A simple flow requests the review and records the outcome.
create-a-document-review-library-pattern.problemStatement: Documents are reviewed over email, nobody knows which copy is current, and approvals cannot be evidenced.
whenToUse: Policies, procedures, proposals and reports that need sign-off
Teams reviewing several documents at once
Evidence of who approved what
whenNotToUse: Formal records management, which needs retention labels and a records centre
Real-time co-authoring with no approval step
create-a-document-review-library-pattern.formulaOrCode:
Library: Documents for Review
  Versioning : major and minor versions; drafts visible to authors and approvers

Columns
  ReviewStatus   Choice   Draft | In review | Changes requested | Approved | Withdrawn   (default Draft, indexed)
  DocumentOwner  Person
  Reviewers      Person (allow multiple)
  ReviewDue      Date
  ReviewComments Multiple lines (append changes)
  ApprovedBy     Person         ApprovedOn  Date
  NextReviewDate Date           for periodic review after approval

Views
  My drafts          : DocumentOwner = [Me] AND ReviewStatus = Draft
  Waiting for me     : Reviewers = [Me] AND ReviewStatus = In review
  In review          : ReviewStatus = In review, sorted by ReviewDue
  Approved           : ReviewStatus = Approved      (the view to link from the intranet)
  Overdue reviews    : ReviewStatus = In review AND ReviewDue < [Today]

Column formatting for ReviewStatus: coloured pills, for example green for Approved, amber for In review.

Flow: request review
  Trigger: When a file is created or modified (properties only)
    Trigger condition: @equals(triggerBody()?['ReviewStatus']?['Value'], 'In review')
  Start and wait for an approval (Approve/Reject - Everyone must approve)
    Assigned to : join the Reviewers' emails with ;
    Item link   : @{triggerBody()?['{Link}']}
  If approved:
    Update file properties: ReviewStatus = Approved, ApprovedBy, ApprovedOn = utcNow(),
                            NextReviewDate = addToTime(utcNow(), 12, 'Month')
    Send an HTTP request to SharePoint to publish a major version:
      POST _api/web/GetFileByServerRelativeUrl('@{triggerBody()?['{Path}']}@{triggerBody()?['{FilenameWithExtension}']}')/publish('Approved')
  If rejected:
    Update file properties: ReviewStatus = Changes requested, ReviewComments = approver comments

Protect approved documents
  Authors edit a new minor version. Readers see the last major version only.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the library with major and minor versioning.
Add review status, owner, reviewers, due date and approval columns.
Build views for drafts, items waiting for the current user, and approved documents.
Add a flow that starts an approval when the status is set to In review and records the result.
Publish a major version on approval so readers always see the approved copy.
commonMistakes: Tracking review status in file names such as v3 FINAL.
Letting readers see drafts.
No due date, so reviews drift.
troubleshooting: If the flow runs on every edit, check the trigger condition and that the flow's own update does not set In review again.
If the Waiting for me view is empty, reviewers were added as a group. [Me] matches individuals.
If readers can see drafts, set draft item security to users who can edit, in versioning settings.
If the publish call fails, the file is checked out or has no minor version to publish.

use-sharepoint-content-types-for-project.shortDescription: Define content types such as Project Plan, Status Report and Change Request so each document type carries its own metadata and template.
use-sharepoint-content-types-for-project.fullDescription: A content type packages a set of columns, a document template and settings under one name. Used in project libraries, it means a status report always has a reporting period and a change request always has an impact, on every project site.
use-sharepoint-content-types-for-project.problemStatement: Every project library has slightly different columns, and documents of different kinds share one flat set of metadata that fits none of them.
whenToUse: Libraries holding several kinds of document
The same document types across many sites
Templates that should open from the New menu
whenNotToUse: A single library with one kind of document
Teams unwilling to fill in metadata
use-sharepoint-content-types-for-project.formulaOrCode:
Content types (parent: Document)
  Project Document           (base for the rest)
      ProjectCode   Single line        Phase   Choice (Initiate, Plan, Deliver, Close)
      DocumentOwner Person
  ├─ Project Plan            + PlanVersion (Text), BaselineDate (Date)
  ├─ Status Report           + ReportingPeriodEnd (Date), OverallRag (Choice)
  ├─ Change Request          + ChangeImpact (Choice), CostImpact (Currency), DecisionStatus (Choice)
  ├─ Meeting Minutes         + MeetingDate (Date), MeetingType (Choice)
  └─ Lessons Learned         + Category (Choice)

Where to create them
  One site        : Site settings > Site content types > Create content type
  Many sites      : SharePoint admin center > Content services > Content type gallery
                    Create, add site columns, then Publish. Sites pick them up through the content type hub.

Steps
  1. Create site columns first (group them under "Project columns").
  2. Create "Project Document" with the shared columns.
  3. Create each child type with Parent = Project Document and add its own columns.
  4. Upload a Word, Excel or PowerPoint template to each type (Advanced settings).
  5. In the library: Library settings > Advanced > Allow management of content types = Yes
     Add from existing site content types. Remove the default "Document" type so users must choose.
  6. Set the order and default under "Change new button order and default content type".

Views
  Status reports : Content Type = Status Report, sort ReportingPeriodEnd descending
  Open changes   : Content Type = Change Request AND DecisionStatus = Pending
  By type        : group by Content Type

Power Automate
  Trigger "When a file is created (properties only)", then a condition on
    triggerBody()?['{ContentType}']?['Name']  equals  'Change Request'
  Set a content type on create: use Send an HTTP request to SharePoint or the ContentTypeId column.

Power Apps
  ThisItem.'Content Type'.Name      // read
  Filtering by content type is not delegable. Mirror it to a choice column if an app needs it.
stepByStepInstructions: List the document types and the metadata each needs.
Create site columns, then a base content type and a child type for each document type.
Attach a template to each type.
Publish from the content type gallery if several sites need them, and add them to each library.
Create views filtered by content type and use the type in flow conditions.
commonMistakes: Creating columns directly in each library, so they cannot be shared.
Too many types with tiny differences.
Leaving the default Document type available, so users skip the choice.
troubleshooting: If a published content type has not reached a site, publishing can take time. Add it from the gallery on the site to pull it immediately.
If uploaded files get the wrong type, drag and drop uses the default type. Set a sensible default or prompt for properties.
If changing a parent type does not update children, tick the option to update all content types inheriting from it.
If an app cannot filter by type, add a choice column that a flow keeps in step with the content type.

build-a-sharepoint-launch-readiness-chec.shortDescription: Run through a go-live checklist for a SharePoint list, app and flows: permissions, performance, support and communications.
build-a-sharepoint-launch-readiness-chec.fullDescription: Most launch problems are predictable: a flow owned by one person, a list that only its maker can see, a view that fails at 5,000 items. This checklist covers what to verify before telling users a solution is live.
